name: Emeka Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. Could you take me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure! I lead a small cell of five CNC mills at Calder Precision, where we cut aluminium and titanium parts for aircraft seats and landing gear brackets. I'm in at 6:30, I look over the overnight programs, and then I spend the morning proving out new jobs and the afternoon troubleshooting whatever broke. Last year I started using an AI assistant to check my G-code and write the setup sheets, and honestly I wonder how I managed without it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the first part off a new program, when it comes out within two hundredths of a millimetre and you know you got it right. What wears me out is the tolerance for waste, because we scrap parts that cost more than my week's pay. And my back, a bit, but I have a good chair for the control desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine with me, because it already helps a bit. It saves me about an hour a day on paperwork, and I'd tell the younger guys to just try it and see. Online I'd probably say it's a good tool, not magic, and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit disappointed, to be honest. I like the feeling that something is moving, and I'd already be thinking about the next skill to pick up. For my job it means I'd keep doing what I do till I retire in four or five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the cell, and I'd keep tidying up my programs with the assistant. I'd also keep teaching a couple of evenings at the community college, because I like it and it pays a bit. And I'd put a couple of hundred a month into the retirement fund, since the cushion at home is only about four months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. Steady, with a bit of boredom. I'm the sort who gets restless when nothing is changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools every day already. What would 'nothing changes' look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would look like now. The assistant checks my code, writes the setup sheets and flags tool wear I might miss. I still decide what to cut and how, so I'm using it like a very quick apprentice who never gets tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And money, in this quiet picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We're okay. My wife Ruth works as a school bursar and we have about four months of savings, plus the house is mostly paid. We help our son Chidi a little with his rent, which I'd keep doing, but the grown-up kids don't need much from us.

say: I'd tell the younger guys to just **try it**, because the assistant already saves me an hour a day.
Online I'd say it's a **good tool**, not magic, and leave it there.
think: I'd be a bit **disappointed**, because I like the feeling that something is moving.
My job would simply continue until I retire in **four or five years**.
do: Keep running my **five-mill cell** and keep checking programs with the assistant.
Keep teaching a couple of evenings at the **community college** for extra income.
Put about **200 a month** into the retirement fund.
feel: **Steady** and comfortable, with a little **boredom** because I like things to be moving.
S0.quote: I still decide what to cut
fieldNote: **Already adapted**: he uses AI daily and sees it as a quick apprentice rather than a threat.
**Restless** when nothing changes, a clue to his appetite for new skills.
**Finances** are moderate, so he adds to the retirement fund even in a calm scenario.

steps.text: Keep running the five-mill cell and checking programs with the assistant
Keep teaching two evenings a week at the community college
Put 200 a month into the retirement fund
Stay in the same job until retirement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the picture I expect, so I'm already getting ready. At work I'd tell the team to learn how the assistant plans a job, because that's the part that changes first. And I'd tell them nobody's out of work yet, but everybody's job gets rewritten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my job gets bigger and a bit different. The programming and planning goes to software, but somebody has to look after the machines, and the robots will want people like me to teach them what a good part looks like. I might become a cell technician, which pays well, and I'd be there early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the robotics course at the technical college and ask Calder Precision to pay for it. I'd start writing up our setups as proper data for the software to learn from, so I'm the one who knows the system. I'd also check what the plant's plan is for older workers, to be safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, and a bit nervous in a good way. It's like when the first CNC machines replaced the manual mills, and I was the young guy who wanted to try them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your own tasks are the thinking tasks that software takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning, the scheduling, the program checks and ordering tools are all thinking tasks. Software already does half of that for me. In a year software would do most of it, and the shop would need fewer programmers and more people who can deal with a stuck robot arm at 2 in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the people on your team who are less keen on this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them it's easier than they think and I'd sit with them for half an hour. A few of the older guys are proud and don't want to look slow. If I say it's a tool and not an exam, they try it, and that's usually enough.

I'd say nobody's out of work yet, but **change** is coming.
think: My job grows and shifts: planning goes to software while I become a **cell technician**.
Robots will need people who know what a **good part** looks like.
do: Sign up for the **robotics course** at the technical college and ask the plant to pay.
Write up our setups as clean **data** so I'm the person who knows the system.
Ask what the plant's plan is for **older workers**, just to be safe.
feel: **Excited** and a bit nervous in a good way, like when the first CNC machines arrived.
fieldNote: **Moves first**: he sees change as an opening and plans a role as cell technician.
**Practical helper**: he coaches older colleagues by calling AI a tool, not an exam.
**Small precaution** about older workers shows he isn't fully relaxed.

steps.text: Sign up for the robotics course at the technical college
Write up our CNC setups as clean data for the planning software
Apply for the cell technician job when it opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we all need to get our heads around this very quickly, and I'd say it without panic. I'd call the union rep and the plant manager and ask what the plan is. Two years is short, so I'd want everybody in one room by Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I think is that this is the real thing, and my thinking work goes first. I'd be 60 when AGI arrives and 63 when robots can do what I do with my hands. That gives me a gap, but it's a tight gap, and the plant might replace my cell earlier than 2031 if the numbers work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut out extras straight away, like the new car I was eyeing, and double my savings rate to build about nine months. I'd ask the plant to move me onto the robot integration project now, and take every course on offer. I'd also work out whether I can retire at 62 on my pension with a small cut, in case the plant closes the cell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A knot in the stomach, which I'm not used to. I like change, but this is change where the timing isn't mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In this picture robots do hands-on work from about 2031. What does the three-year gap give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years is the time to become the person who works with the robots, not the person replaced by them. I'd use all of it. If I can service and train the robot, I keep a job. If I can't, I'm a 63-year-old with four months of savings, and that's a bad place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter Ada to stay in her public health job, since it's about people. And my son Chidi should stay close to the work that has thinking and hands in it together, like his work testing software for medical equipment. And I'd tell both of them I'll be fine, even if I'm only 80 percent sure.

say: I'd say we need to get our heads around this **quickly**, without panic, and call the union rep and plant manager.
I'd want everybody in one room by **Friday**.
think: My thinking work goes first in **2028**, and the cell could be replaced before 2031.
The gap is **tight**, so I need to become the person who works with robots.
do: Drop extras like the car I was eyeing and aim for **nine months** of savings.
Ask to join the **robot integration project** now and take every course on offer.
Work out whether I can **retire at 62** with a small pension cut.
feel: A **knot in my stomach**, which is new, because this is change where the timing isn't mine.
S2.quote: Three years is the time to become the person who works with the robots, not the person replaced by them.
fieldNote: **Adaptable but exposed**: he plans to join robot integration but admits the gap is tight.
**Money** is the weak point, with moderate savings and no wish to be stuck at 63.
**Honest with family**: he'd tell his kids he's fine though only partly sure.

steps.text: Skip the new car and double the monthly savings rate
Build savings to about nine months of expenses
Ask to join the plant's robot integration project this month
Check the pension numbers for retiring at 62

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is manageable if we work on it now. I'd tell my team that five years is enough to become the best-trained group in the region, and I'd put my money on that. People who sit and wait will have a harder time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm optimistic. The thinking AI arrives when I'm 63 and robots when I'm 66, so I'd have already moved into robot maintenance by then, or be retired. I'd still worry for the younger machinists whose whole trade is hands-on, but they have time to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year learning robot programming at night school and ask the plant to give me a trial robot cell. I'd save about 400 a month, and I'd start offering CNC workshops at the community college for a bit of side money. By year three I'd know whether to stay on as a technician or retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty hopeful. A bit of excitement, a bit of tiredness thinking about night school at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, is there a plan you'd run differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd move gradually, not in a panic. I'd learn robot programming and teach a bit, and still have room to adjust if something unexpected happens. That's the difference compared with two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry about anyone at Calder Precision in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My apprentice Dmitri, who's 24 and brilliant with his hands but doesn't use any software. I'd sit him down and say learn the assistant now, while it's easy. I'd also want the plant to commit to retraining him, not just letting him go.

say: I'd tell my team five years is enough to become the **best-trained group** in the region.
People who **sit and wait** will have the hardest time.
think: I'm **optimistic**: by the time robots reach my work I'd have moved into maintenance or retired.
I'd still worry about **younger machinists** whose trade is purely hands-on.
do: Learn **robot programming** at night school and ask for a trial robot cell.
Save about **400 a month** and run CNC workshops for side money.
Decide by year three whether to stay as a **technician** or retire.
feel: **Hopeful**, with a little excitement and some tiredness at the idea of night school.
S3.quote: five years is enough to become the best-trained group in the region, and I'd put my money on that.
fieldNote: **Time suits him**: five years lets him move gradually instead of scrambling.

**Side income** is a deliberate extra pillar, not just a hobby.

steps.text: Learn robot programming at night school in the first year
Save 400 a month for the next five years
Run paid CNC workshops at the community college
Coach apprentice Dmitri on the planning assistant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best of the three AGI cases, because it gives everyone time to move. I'd say it at the plant, and also to the town council, because ten years isn't long for training programmes to be built. Somebody has to start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I think is that I'd probably retire before robots get to my work in 2039. So for me it's a quiet story, but I find it exciting for the young ones. It might be a golden age for people who combine craft and software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as a cell lead for three or four more years, then wind down into part-time teaching. I'd put more into the retirement fund. And I'd set up a small side shop in the garage with one used mill, to make parts for local clubs and small firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty happy about it. A little curious about what the world looks like in ten years, and I'd like to see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, you'd be past retirement. What would you do with the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the used mill in the garage, and I'd use the assistant to quote jobs and plan the work. It's a hobby, and a small income, and I'd keep my hands in the metal after the plant. That's what I'd want retirement to look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a 25-year-old starting as a machinist today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn the machine and the software together. Don't pick one. A person who can run a mill and also talk to the AI that plans the work will have a job for a long time, and a good one.

say: I'd say this is the **best case**, but ten years isn't long to build training programmes.
I'd tell the town council to **start now**.
think: I'd probably **retire** before robots reach my work in 2039, so for me it's a quiet story.
It could be a **golden age** for people who combine craft and software.
do: Work as cell lead three or four more years, then go **part-time teaching**.
Set up a garage shop with one **used mill** for local clubs and small firms.
feel: **Happy** and curious about what the world looks like in ten years.
S4.quote: A person who can run a mill
fieldNote: **Comfortable**: with ten years he's thinking about a garage shop, not survival.
**Craft plus software** is his consistent advice for young people.
**Retirement vision** keeps his hands in metal through a small side business.

steps.text: Work three or four more years as cell lead, then teach part-time
Set up a garage shop making parts for local clubs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd cope, but it doesn't leave time to build the next version of myself. What would help is a company that pays for training on work time, and a pension rule that doesn't punish me for going early if my cell closes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what excites me. A tool that reads a drawing and suggests a cutting strategy is cool. I'd like the older guys to feel the same, and not be left behind because nobody sat down with them for half an hour.

headlineQuote: A tool that reads a drawing
portrait: **Emeka** is a 58-year-old CNC cell lead at an aircraft parts shop, a few years from retirement.
He uses **AI every day**, calls it a quick apprentice, and sees change as a chance to become a robot-cell technician.
His wife works as a school bursar, and about **four months** of savings is his main weak point.
He stays calm in most pictures and turns **uneasy** only in the two-year world, where the gap before robots is tight.
biggestWorry: The **two-year scenario**, because there's no time to build the next version of himself.
whatWouldHelp: Company-paid **training on work time**, and a pension rule that doesn't punish early exit if his cell closes.
